questions.question: A rotating coil in a school a.c. generator is connected across an LED. Explain why the LED flashes on and off as the coil rotates.
questions.answer: The induced e.m.f. alternates in direction; the LED is a diode that conducts in one direction only, so it lights only on alternate half-cycles.
steps: As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux linkage through it changes continuously.
By Faraday's law, an e.m.f. is induced whose size depends on the rate of change of flux linkage.
The flux linkage changes sign over each half turn, so the induced e.m.f. reverses direction (Lenz's law).
The output is therefore an alternating e.m.f., and the current in the circuit reverses each half cycle.
An LED is a diode, which conducts only in its forward direction.
So the LED is lit only during the half-cycles when the current flows forward, giving a flashing effect.

questions.question: Explain the changes to the V-t graph of the generator output when the angular velocity of the coil is halved.
questions.answer: The peak p.d. halves and the period doubles (frequency halves), so the trace is half as tall and twice as long.
steps: Peak induced e.m.f. = NBA omega, so it is directly proportional to angular velocity omega.
Halving omega therefore halves the peak p.d. (amplitude).
Period T = 2 pi / omega, so halving omega doubles the period.
Frequency is halved because f = 1/T.
On the graph the waveform becomes half as tall and stretched to twice the time length.

questions.question: A lever is rotated through 90 degrees by a force that rises steadily from 2.6 N to 9.6 N, applied at right angles to a 4.9 cm lever. Show the work done is about 0.5 J.
questions.answer: W = 0.47 J, which is about 0.5 J as required.
steps: The force increases steadily (linearly), so the average force is (2.6 + 9.6)/2 = 6.1 N.
A rotation of 90 degrees is pi/2 radians.
The force is at right angles to the lever, so the distance moved is the arc length s = r theta = 0.049 x pi/2 = 0.0770 m.
Work done = average force x distance = 6.1 x 0.0770 = 0.47 J.
0.47 J rounds to about 0.5 J, as shown.

questions.question: Explain how an alternating p.d. across the input coil of an iron-cored transformer causes a capacitor to charge through a diode on the output coil.
questions.answer: The alternating input current gives a changing flux in the core, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in the output coil; the diode passes only one half-cycle, so the capacitor charges.
steps: The alternating p.d. drives an alternating current in the input coil.
This alternating current produces a changing magnetic flux in the shared iron core.
The changing flux links the output coil, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in it (mutual induction, Faraday's law).
The diode conducts only in one direction, so only one polarity of the output reaches the capacitor (half-wave rectification).
Charge flows onto the capacitor during each forward half-cycle, and the diode stops it discharging back.
Over many cycles charge builds up, so the capacitor charges to a high p.d. and stores energy.

questions.question: Explain how steadily increasing the current in the central coil of a tokamak produces a current in the plasma.
questions.answer: The increasing coil current gives a changing flux through the plasma loop, which induces an e.m.f. and so a current in the conducting plasma.
steps: Steadily increasing the current in the central coil increases the magnetic field it produces.
The magnetic flux through the plasma loop, which surrounds the coil, therefore increases steadily.
By Faraday's law, a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in the loop.
The plasma is an electrical conductor, so the e.m.f. drives a current around it.

questions.question: A magnet falls through a copper tube suspended from a force meter and the meter reading increases. Explain why.
questions.answer: Induced eddy currents in the copper oppose the falling magnet, so the magnet pushes the tube downwards, adding to the reading.
steps: As the magnet falls, the magnetic flux through the copper tube changes.
This induces eddy currents, which are closed loops of current in the copper.
By Lenz's law, the eddy currents oppose the change that produces them.
The eddy currents' magnetic field pushes the magnet upward, opposing its fall.
By Newton's third law, the magnet exerts an equal downward force on the tube.
This extra downward force adds to the tube's weight, so the force meter reading increases.

questions.question: The flux density through a coil is increased steadily from zero to a maximum. Which single change would give a smaller current in the resistor?

The current in the resistor I = E / R, so a smaller rate of change gives a smaller current.

B: a larger maximum B increases the rate of change over the same time, so the current increases.
D: a longer time reduces the rate of change of flux, so the current is smaller.

questions.question: Assuming no resistive forces, deduce whether the carriage (leaving at about 40 m s-1) reaches the top of an 81 m tower.
questions.answer: Yes: the maximum height is about 90 m, which is greater than 81 m.
steps: With no resistive forces, the kinetic energy at the base converts fully to gravitational potential energy.
Using v = 42.1 m s-1: mgh = (1/2) m v^2, so h = v^2 / (2g).
90 m is greater than the 81 m tower height, so the carriage reaches the top (with about 9 m to spare).

questions.question: Explain why an aluminium fin leaves the gap between magnets at a much slower speed than it entered.
questions.answer: Eddy currents in the moving aluminium oppose its motion (Lenz's law) and the kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy.
steps: As the fin moves through the magnetic field, the flux through it changes.
This induces eddy currents in the aluminium fin.
The eddy currents are in a magnetic field, so they experience a force (F = BIL).
By Lenz's law this force opposes the motion of the fin, so it decelerates.
Work done against this force transfers kinetic energy into thermal energy (I^2 R heating) in the aluminium.
So the fin loses kinetic energy and leaves the gap much more slowly.

questions.question: Explain why a current was produced in the aluminium plate as it passed between the poles of the magnet.

By electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law), an e.m.f. is induced in the plate.

questions.question: Explain why the kinetic energy of the vehicle decreases as the aluminium plate moves between the magnet poles.
questions.answer: The eddy currents experience a force that opposes motion (Lenz's law); work done against it is transferred to thermal energy in the plate.
steps: The eddy currents in the plate are in the magnetic field, so they experience a magnetic force.
By Lenz's law this force opposes the motion of the plate.
Work is done against this opposing force as the plate moves.

questions.question: Suggest why the percentage reduction in kinetic energy increases as the thickness of the aluminium plate increases.

steps: Resistance of the plate R = rho L / A, and a thicker plate has a larger cross-sectional area A.
So a thicker plate has lower resistance.
The induced e.m.f. is the same, so the eddy current I = e.m.f./R is larger.
A larger eddy current gives a larger magnetic braking force (F = BIL), so more energy is transferred to thermal energy.
A larger fraction of the kinetic energy is therefore lost.

questions.answer: The suggestion is valid: the changing flux induces eddy currents, and by Lenz's law the disc is dragged in the same direction as the magnet moves relative to it.
steps: Moving the magnet around the disc changes the magnetic flux through the disc, so eddy currents are induced in it.

The disc therefore starts to rotate, in the same direction as the magnet is moved.
The disc never quite reaches the speed of the magnet, because a relative motion is needed to induce the currents.

questions.question: A strong magnet falls through two copper tubes of equal length and area; tube B has a vertical slit. Discuss the difference in fall times.
questions.answer: The magnet falls more slowly through solid tube A, because eddy currents can circulate around it; the slit in tube B blocks the loops, so B has smaller eddy currents and the magnet falls faster.
steps: Falling magnet changes the flux through the copper; eddy currents are induced in the tube (Faraday's law).
In tube A the eddy currents can circulate completely around the tube, so they are large.
By Lenz's law the large eddy currents produce a large upward force, which slows the magnet.
The vertical slit in tube B interrupts the circulating path, so the eddy currents are much smaller.
The braking force is therefore smaller in B, so the magnet falls faster and takes less time through tube B.
Tube A gives the longer fall time.

questions.question: Using Lenz's law, explain why the current in the primary coil does not reach its maximum value instantaneously when the switch is closed.

steps: When the switch closes, the current increases and so does the flux in the coil core.
The changing flux induces an e.m.f. in the same coil (self-induction).
By Lenz's law, this induced e.m.f. opposes the change that causes it (a back e.m.f.).
The back e.m.f. reduces the net p.d. driving the current, so the current rises gradually to its maximum.

questions.question: A 90 m power cable carries 700 A. Near the pylons the Earth's field is 48 uT at 20 degrees to the vertical. Determine the force on the cable.
questions.answer: Pending: the angle between the cable and the field depends on the diagram; the force is B I L sin(theta).

questions.question: A key card with bar magnets is pulled through a card reader with a coil and voltage sensor. Explain how the sensor detects the orientation of the magnetic poles.
questions.answer: Each magnet's field produces a change in flux through the coil as it passes; the polarity of the induced voltage depends on the pole orientation.
steps: As the card moves through the reader, each magnet's field passes through the coil and changes the flux linkage.
By Faraday's law, each change induces a voltage across the coil.
Reversing a magnet's pole reverses the direction of its field, so the flux change has the opposite sign.
The sensor therefore sees a voltage of positive or negative polarity for each magnet, showing its pole orientation.

questions.question: The card moves 9.0 cm in 0.032 s. Using 25 turns, B = 2.4 x 10^-5 T and magnet width 0.98 mm, deduce whether the induced voltage exceeds 1.5 x 10^-6 V.
questions.answer: Yes: the induced e.m.f. is about 1.7 x 10^-6 V, which is greater than 1.5 x 10^-6 V.
steps: Speed of card v = 0.090 m / 0.032 s = 2.81 m s-1.
Use E = N B w v, where w is the magnet width (0.98 x 10^-3 m).
Since 1.65 x 10^-6 V > 1.5 x 10^-6 V, the card reader can determine the pole orientation.

questions.question: A proton experiences a force of 6.5 x 10^-13 N in a field of B = 0.52 T. Calculate its speed.
questions.answer: v = 7.8 x 10^6 m s-1 (assuming the proton enters perpendicular to the field)
steps: Magnetic force on a charge F = B q v for velocity perpendicular to the field.
Rearrange: v = F / (B q).

questions.question: Explain how a mobile phone charges when placed near a wireless charger that has an alternating current in a coil.
questions.answer: The alternating current in the charger coil produces a changing flux that links the phone's coil, inducing an alternating e.m.f. which is rectified to charge the battery.
steps: The alternating current in the charger's coil produces a changing magnetic flux.
Some of this flux links the coil in the phone (mutual induction).
By Faraday's law, the changing flux induces an alternating e.m.f. in the phone's coil.
The phone's circuit rectifies this alternating e.m.f. to a direct p.d., which charges the battery.

questions.question: The coil on the a.c. supply has 50 turns of diameter 4.0 cm, with a maximum B of 18 mT. Calculate its maximum flux linkage.
questions.answer: Flux linkage = 1.1 x 10^-3 Wb
steps: Radius r = 4.0 cm / 2 = 0.020 m, so area A = pi r^2 = 1.26 x 10^-3 m^2.
Flux per turn at maximum = B A = 0.018 x 1.26 x 10^-3 = 2.26 x 10^-5 Wb.
Flux linkage = N B A = 50 x 2.26 x 10^-5 = 1.13 x 10^-3 Wb.
The maximum flux linkage is 1.1 x 10^-3 Wb.

questions.question: Suggest why the maximum p.d. across the voltmeter coil is less than the maximum p.d. of the a.c. supply.
questions.answer: Not all the flux from the supply coil links the second coil (flux leakage), so the induced p.d. is smaller.
steps: The two coils are not perfectly coupled, so some flux from the supply coil does not pass through the second coil.
Since the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the flux linked, the induced p.d. is smaller than the supply p.d.

questions.question: A wire of length 40 mm carries 3.1 A in a field between magnets, and the balance reading increases by 0.45 g. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
steps: Force on the wire equals the balance increase: F = 4.5 x 10^-4 kg x 9.81 = 4.41 x 10^-3 N.
Force on a conductor perpendicular to the field: F = B I L.
